Feast of Trumpets
FEEST of TRUM-pets
n. phrase
Trumpets: the silver trumpets and ram’s horn (shophar) blown to inaugurate the day. Hebrew yōm teru‘ah (day of blowing) or zīkhrōn teru‘ah (memorial of blowing); the OT festival prescribed in Leviticus 23:23-25, observed on the first day of the seventh month (Tishri 1; later called Rosh Hashanah).

See also: Feast of Trumpets · Feast of Trumpets

📖 Biblical Definition

The Feast of Trumpets was the OT festival inaugurating the seventh month (Tishri), the most sacred month of the Jewish religious year. Leviticus 23:23-25 prescribes the observance: in the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation. Ye shall do no servile work therein: but ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD. Numbers 29:1-6 adds detail on the burnt offerings and meal offerings. The day was marked by the blowing of trumpets (likely both the silver trumpets of Num 10 and the ram’s horn shophar); the cessation of ordinary work; the assembly of the people in holy convocation; and the offering of a young bullock, a ram, and seven lambs of the first year as burnt offerings, with the accompanying meal offerings and the daily and monthly sacrifices. The Feast of Trumpets inaugurated the most solemn ten-day period of the Jewish year, leading to the Day of Atonement on Tishri 10 and the Feast of Tabernacles beginning on Tishri 15. Later Jewish tradition came to call the Feast of Trumpets Rosh Hashanah (head of the year) and to associate it with the day of judgment and the heavenly opening of the books in which the year’s decrees are written—though these later associations go beyond the explicit OT specification. The typological substance of trumpets in biblical theology is extensive. Trumpets in Scripture sound at several great moments. The giving of the Law at Sinai was accompanied by the exceeding loud trumpet (Ex 19:16, 19; 20:18); the LORD’s coming-down to Sinai was marked by the trumpet of God. The trumpet calls Israel to war (Num 10:9). The trumpet announces the year of jubilee (Lev 25:9). The trumpet calls the assembly (Num 10:7). And in the New Testament, the trumpet is the apocalyptic signal of the Lord’s return. 1 Thessalonians 4:16: for the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first. 1 Corinthians 15:52: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. Matthew 24:31: and he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds. The Feast of Trumpets therefore typologically anticipates the eschatological trumpet of the Lord’s return, which gathers His people, raises the dead in Christ, transforms the living, and inaugurates the consummation of redemption.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines TRUMPET as a wind instrument of music, in the form of a long tube curved at one or two places; in scripture, the Feast of Trumpets (Lev 23:23-25) inaugurated the seventh month, typologically anticipating the eschatological trumpet of the Lord’s return (1 Thess 4:16; 1 Cor 15:52).

TRUMPET, n. — A wind instrument of music, in the form of a long tube curved at one or two places. In scripture, used for calling the assembly, for war, for the announcement of feasts, and (eschatologically) for the Lord’s coming.

FEAST OF TRUMPETS — A solemn festival of the Jews, observed on the first day of the seventh month, marked by the blowing of trumpets; the inauguration of the most sacred month of the Jewish year (Lev 23:23-25).

📖 Key Scripture

Leviticus 23:24-25 — "Speak unto the children of Israel, saying, In the seventh month, in the first day of the month, shall ye have a sabbath, a memorial of blowing of trumpets, an holy convocation. Ye shall do no servile work therein: but ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD."

1 Thessalonians 4:16 — "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first."

1 Corinthians 15:52 — "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed."

Matthew 24:31 — "And he shall send his angels with a great sound of a trumpet, and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from one end of heaven to the other."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Feast of Trumpets is corrupted, on one side, by the general loss of OT festal typology that has dropped its eschatological significance—and on the other by the speculative-date-setting tradition (especially in some dispensational and rapture-focused circles) that has attempted to pinpoint the rapture to the Feast of Trumpets in a specific year, against Christ’s explicit teaching that no man knoweth the day or hour.

expand to see more

The general loss of OT festal typology has dropped the Feast of Trumpets from contemporary preaching as obscure cultic detail without operative theological substance. The festival’s typological substance, however, is significant: trumpets in the biblical theology are the eschatological signal of the Lord’s great acts—the Law-giving at Sinai, the announcement of jubilee, the call to war, the gathering of the assembly, and ultimately the trumpet of the Lord’s return. The Feast of Trumpets sat at the head of the most solemn month of the Jewish year and anticipated the eschatological trumpet that would inaugurate the consummation. The recovery is the recovery of the typology. The trumpet of the Lord’s return is anticipated in the trumpets of Sinai, of Jericho, of jubilee, and of the seventh-month Feast of Trumpets; the saint listening for the eschatological trumpet hears it sounding from across the entire OT festal calendar.

The opposite corruption is the speculative-date-setting tradition that has, especially in some dispensational and rapture-focused circles, attempted to pinpoint the rapture to the Feast of Trumpets in a specific year. The reasoning typically goes: the rapture will involve a trumpet (1 Thess 4:16; 1 Cor 15:52); the Feast of Trumpets is the OT festival of trumpet-blowing; the typological connection suggests the rapture will occur on the Feast of Trumpets in a specific calendar year; therefore the date of the rapture is calculable. Christ Himself forecloses this entire reasoning: but of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only (Matt 24:36). The typological connection between the Feast of Trumpets and the eschatological trumpet is real; the inference to a specific date is forbidden. The recovery is the recovery of both: the typological substance (the Feast of Trumpets does anticipate the trumpet of the Lord’s coming) and the apostolic restraint (the date is not given to us, and speculation is not the right response). The Christian waits, watches, and prepares for the trumpet’s sound in faithful daily discipleship, not in date-setting speculation that Christ Himself forbade.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yōm teru‘ah (day of blowing) or zīkhrōn teru‘ah (memorial of blowing); the OT festival of the seventh month’s first day; typologically anticipating the eschatological trumpet of the Lord’s return at which the dead in Christ shall rise and the living shall be changed (1 Thess 4:16; 1 Cor 15:52).

expand to see more

Hebrew teru‘ah (H8643) — blowing, shouting (the noun behind the festival’s name).

Hebrew shōphār (H7782) — ram’s horn (the chief trumpet of the festival).

Hebrew chatsōts’rāh (H2689) — silver trumpet (Num 10:1-10; the trumpet of the priests).

Greek salpinx (G4536) — trumpet (the eschatological trumpet of 1 Cor 15:52; 1 Thess 4:16; Matt 24:31; Rev 8-9).

Usage

"For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God—the eschatological trumpet that the Feast of Trumpets anticipates."

"The Feast of Trumpets inaugurated the most sacred month of the Jewish year, leading to the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles."

"Loss of typology drops the festal substance; date-setting speculation attempts to pinpoint the rapture to a specific Feast of Trumpets; biblical doctrine holds the typology while preserving Christ’s explicit restraint against date-setting."
